questions.q: After launching a request for proposals for the organic catering project they’re leading, a project manager is assessing four potential suppliers by ranking them based on three main aspects: the quality of their products, their production capacity, and their costs. Which of the following selection techniques is being used by the project manager? *

o.t: Screening system
Evaluation criteria
Weighting system
Contract negotiation

questions.e: The weighting system is a supplier selection technique where various factors (such as quality, production capacity, and costs) are assigned different weights based on their importance to the project. The suppliers are then evaluated and scored on each of these factors, and the scores are multiplied by the assigned weights to determine an overall ranking. This approach allows for a more comprehensive and balanced assessment of the potential suppliers by considering multiple aspects of their offerings.

questions.q: You are managing a construction project. Four sellers have sent proposals as a response to the RFP that the procurement department in your organization sent. You need to gain a more objective understanding of sellers' capabilities in order to rank their proposals and select the best one. Which technique may best help avoid bias and subjective decisions? *

o.t: Independent estimates.
Negotiation.
Bidder conference.
Weighting system.

questions.e: The weighting system is a technique used to objectively evaluate and rank proposals by assigning different weights to various criteria (e.g., price, quality, delivery time). Each proposal is scored against these criteria, and the scores are multiplied by the assigned weights to determine an overall ranking. This method helps to avoid bias and subjective decisions by providing a structured and quantifiable way to compare the capabilities of different sellers.

questions.q: You are managing a risky construction project. Your organization has a bad history of dealing with risky projects and none of your team members has experience in working with this type of projects. You decide to acquire a risk management expert to help you reduce the overall project risk to be below the acceptable risk threshold. Which type of contract is most appropriate for your organization to sign with be expert? *

o.t: FFP.
CPIF.
FPEPA.
T&M.

questions.e: A Time and Materials (T&M) contract is most appropriate in this scenario because it allows flexibility in the payment for the expert's services. T&M contracts are suitable for projects where the scope of work is not well-defined and may evolve over time, which is often the case with risky projects that require expertise to manage uncertainties. This type of contract will enable you to pay for the actual time and resources expended by the risk management expert, providing the flexibility needed to address the project's risks effectively.

questions.q: All of the following statements about bidder conference are true except: *

o.t: The buyer should meet each potential seller separately.
Bidder conferences are held prior to proposal submittal.
Bidder conferences are also called contractor conferences, vendor conferences, and pre-bid conferences.
All sellers receive the same procurement documents.

questions.e: Bidder conferences are meetings held with all potential sellers to ensure that all of them have a clear and common understanding of the procurement requirements and to clarify any questions they might have. Meeting each potential seller separately would undermine the purpose of the bidder conference, which is to ensure transparency and fairness by providing the same information to all bidders simultaneously.

questions.q: Phillip is managing a research and development project. The scope of the project is not clear, so he decided to outsource the project work to another company. He agreed with the procurement manager to use the cost plus incentive fee (CPIF) contract. All of the following are true about this type of contract except: *

o.t: The seller receives all costs of the performed contractual work, in addition to a predetermined incentive fee based upon achieving certain performance objectives.
If the final costs are less or greater than the original estimated costs, the both the buyer and seller share costs from the departures based upon a pre-negotiated cost-sharing formula.
This type of contract should be used if the scope of work is expected to change significantly during the execution of the contract.
The total cost of the contract is known and agreed upon before starting the work.

questions.e: In a Cost Plus Incentive Fee (CPIF) contract, the total cost of the contract is not known and agreed upon before starting the work. The seller is reimbursed for all legitimate costs incurred during the project and receives an additional incentive fee based on performance objectives. The total cost can vary, and any cost savings or overruns are shared between the buyer and seller according to a pre-negotiated formula. Therefore, statement D is not true about CPIF contracts.

questions.q: To obtain the human resource requirements of your new project, you published a job offer on a well-known recruitment platform. Days later, you received over 300 applications. Going through all of them will take a lot of time and effort, so what’s the best next course of action? *

o.t: Use a weighting system to select the best applicants.
Add a section for minimum qualifications in the job description.
Create a screening system to reduce the number of applications to treat.
Randomly select a few candidates and pick the best of them.

questions.e: Creating a screening system allows you to efficiently narrow down the large pool of applicants to a manageable number based on predefined criteria, such as relevant experience, qualifications, and skills. This system helps ensure that only the most suitable candidates move forward in the selection process, saving time and effort while maintaining a high standard of selection.

questions.q: A team receives outsourced deliverables and determines that they do not meet the agreed-upon acceptance criteria. What should the project manager reference to verify this with the vendor? *

o.t: Procurement management plan
Request for proposal (RFP)
Statement of work (SOW)
Inspections

questions.e: The Statement of Work (SOW) outlines the specific deliverables, acceptance criteria, and performance standards agreed upon between the buyer and the vendor. By referencing the SOW, the project manager can verify whether the delivered work meets the agreed-upon requirements and acceptance criteria.

questions.q: A contracted project manager is leading a project using a predictive approach. The project sponsor is disappointed with the progress so far, claiming that a critical deliverable has been overlooked. Although they approved all project stages to date, they asked the project manager to put the project on hold until they reassess the situation. To reach an agreement, the project manager decided to use arbitration and mediation as: (choose two) *

o.t: Dispute resolution techniques
Coaching techniques
Assisted negotiation techniques
Direct negotiation techniques
Negotiation facilitation techniques

questions.e: Dispute resolution techniques: Arbitration and mediation are commonly used techniques to resolve disputes between parties. They involve a third party to help reach a mutually acceptable solution. Assisted negotiation techniques: These techniques involve a neutral third party to assist the disputing parties in negotiating a resolution. Both arbitration and mediation fall under this category as they help facilitate negotiations.

questions.q: Your organization is a bidder in a new office building project and you are assigned to prepare the bidding document project. Your organization will provide furniture for the buyer. You need to know more details about the specifications of the needed furniture because the statement of work which the buyer sent is not detailed enough. Which document will you send to the buyer in this situation? *

o.t: Procurement statement of work (SOW).
Request for proposal (RFP).
Request for quotation (RFQ).
Request for information (RFI).

questions.e: A Request for Information (RFI) is used when you need more details about the specifications, requirements, or other aspects of a project that are not clear. It helps the bidder understand the buyer's needs more clearly before submitting a more detailed proposal or quotation. This is appropriate in this scenario where the statement of work (SOW) provided by the buyer is not detailed enough.

questions.q: Pascal is a project manager for a large construction project. All the project work will be outsourced to other subcontractors. Pascal is just starting the procurement process. Which of the following should be done last? *

o.t: Seek expert judgment from a variety of resources.
Select contract type whether FP, T&M or CR.
Perform make-or-buy analysis.
Finalize the terms and conditions of the contract.

questions.e: Finalizing the terms and conditions of the contract is typically one of the last steps in the procurement process. Before reaching this point, a project manager would seek expert judgment, select the appropriate contract type, and perform a make-or-buy analysis to determine whether outsourcing is the best option. Only after these steps would the terms and conditions of the contract be finalized to ensure that all requirements and agreements are clearly documented and agreed upon.

questions.q: A project manager is conducting a bidder conference to ensure that all potential vendors have a clear understanding of the project requirements. What is the primary purpose of a bidder conference? *

o.t: To negotiate contract terms with the preferred vendor.
To provide all bidders with equal information and clarify project requirements.
To finalize the selection of a vendor before contract award.
To allow vendors to present their proposals before selection.

questions.e: A bidder conference (also called a pre-bid meeting) ensures all potential vendors receive the same information and clarifications, promoting fairness and competition. Negotiations (A) occur after vendor selection. Finalizing vendor selection (C) happens after proposal evaluations. Vendor presentations (D) occur in proposal reviews, not the bidder conference.

questions.q: During a bidder conference, a vendor tries to persuade the project manager by offering additional services at a discounted rate. How should the project manager respond? *

o.t: Accept the offer if it benefits the project.
Inform all bidders about the offer to maintain fairness.
Reject the offer and remind the vendor that the bidding process must remain fair.
Allow the vendor to submit an updated proposal after the conference.

questions.e: Bidder conferences must remain neutral. Offering additional services during the meeting could lead to an unfair selection process. Informing all bidders (B) does not address the fairness concern directly. Accepting the offer (A, D) violates procurement integrity.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a key ethical consideration during a bidder conference? *

o.t: Ensuring that only preferred vendors receive key project details.
Allowing bidders to submit additional documents after the deadline.
Maintaining transparency by providing the same information to all bidders.
Encouraging bidders to modify their pricing based on discussions in the conference.

questions.e: A bidder conference must ensure fair competition by providing equal access to information for all vendors. Providing details only to preferred vendors (A) is unethical. Allowing late document submissions (B) gives unfair advantages. Encouraging pricing changes (D) can lead to unfair practices.

questions.q: A company needs to select a vendor for a project with a limited budget. Several vendors meet the minimum requirements, and the company wants to choose the lowest-priced option. Which vendor selection method should be used? *

o.t: Best Value Selection
Least Cost Selection
Weighted Scoring Model
Sole Sourcing

questions.e: Least Cost Selection is used when all vendors meet requirements, and cost is the primary decision factor. Best Value Selection (A) considers both quality and cost. Weighted Scoring (C) evaluates multiple factors, not just cost. Sole Sourcing (D) is used when only one vendor is available.

questions.q: A project requires specialized equipment that only one vendor can provide. The project manager must select a vendor quickly to avoid delays. What is the most appropriate selection method? *

o.t: Sole Sourcing
Competitive Bidding
Best Value Selection
Reverse Auction

questions.e: Sole sourcing is used when only one vendor can provide the required product or service. Competitive Bidding (B) is for multiple vendors. Best Value (C) compares multiple factors but is unnecessary when there’s only one option. Reverse Auction (D) is for cost-based selection, which does not apply to a single vendor.

questions.q: A project manager is reviewing vendor proposals and realizes that vendors have submitted different formats, making it difficult to compare them. What should the project manager have done to ensure a fair vendor evaluation? *

o.t: Require vendors to submit proposals in a standard template.
Allow flexibility in proposal formats to encourage creativity.
Select the vendor with the most detailed proposal.
Request additional information from selected vendors only.

questions.e: A standard template ensures consistency, making it easier to compare vendor proposals. Allowing flexibility (B) can lead to inconsistent data. Selecting based on proposal detail (C) ignores fair evaluation principles. Requesting additional info only from some vendors (D) creates bias.

questions.q: A project manager is working with a vendor responsible for manufacturing a critical component. Before approving shipment, the project team visits the vendor’s facility to verify that the product meets quality standards. What type of vendor inspection is this? *

o.t: Pre-shipment Inspection
In-Process Inspection
Post-Delivery Inspection
Acceptance Testing

questions.e: A pre-shipment inspection is conducted before a vendor ships goods to verify quality and compliance with project requirements. In-process inspections (B) occur during manufacturing, not before shipment. Post-delivery inspections (C) take place after receipt. Acceptance testing (D) is conducted after delivery but typically in software or product validation contexts.

questions.q: A vendor delivers equipment to a project site, but the project team discovers defects upon inspection. What should the project manager do first? *

o.t: Issue a formal non-conformance report (NCR) to the vendor.
Reject the equipment and request immediate replacement.
Escalate the issue to senior management.
Allow project work to continue while addressing the issue later.

questions.e: A non-conformance report (NCR) formally documents defects and requests corrective action from the vendor. Rejecting the equipment immediately (B) may be necessary but should follow formal procedures. Escalation (C) is premature without vendor engagement. Continuing work with defective equipment (D) risks project failure.

questions.q: A project manager is overseeing a construction project where the total cost is uncertain due to fluctuating material prices. The client wants to control costs while providing some flexibility for price changes. Which contract type is most appropriate? *

o.t: Firm Fixed Price (FFP)
Cost Plus Fixed Fee (CPFF)
Fixed Price with Economic Price Adjustment (FP-EPA)
Time and Materials (T&M)

questions.e: FP-EPA contracts allow adjustments for price fluctuations due to market conditions, making them suitable for projects affected by inflation or material cost variations. FFP (A) is not ideal since prices are fixed with no flexibility. CPFF (B) reimburses costs but does not provide price protection. T&M (D) is for work with undefined scope, not price-sensitive contracts.

questions.q: A project manager is working with multiple vendors and wants to ensure contract compliance throughout execution. What is the best approach? *

o.t: Conduct regular contract performance reviews.
Require vendors to submit weekly progress reports.
Escalate any vendor issues to procurement management.
Apply penalties for any minor contract deviations.

questions.e: Regular reviews ensure compliance and prevent issues from escalating. Weekly reports (B) provide updates but do not replace full compliance checks. Escalation (C) should be reserved for major issues. Strict penalties (D) may harm vendor relationships.

questions.q: A vendor submits an invoice that exceeds the agreed contract price, citing additional work. The project manager did not authorize any changes. What should the project manager do? *

o.t: Approve partial payment while investigating the discrepancy.
Reject the invoice and request an explanation.
Escalate the issue to the finance department.
Approve full payment to maintain vendor relations.

questions.e: Unapproved additional work should not be paid for without justification. Partial payment (A) sets a bad precedent. Escalating (C) is unnecessary before resolving with the vendor. Approving full payment (D) could lead to cost overruns.

questions.q: A vendor claims additional payment is required due to unexpected project complexity, but the contract does not mention this. What should the project manager do first? *

o.t: Approve the request to maintain vendor relationships.
Review the contract to confirm whether additional payments are justified.
Deny the request immediately, as it is not in the contract.
Escalate the issue to senior management.

questions.e: Contracts define payment terms; reviewing them helps determine the validity of the claim. Approving extra costs (A) without verification risks budget overruns. Denying (C) is premature without analysis. Escalation (D) should come after reviewing contract details.

questions.q: A vendor has completed work, but the project team identifies defects during inspection. The vendor claims they have met contract specifications. What should the project manager do? *

o.t: Approve the work since the contract was followed.
Issue a non-conformance report and request corrective action.
Terminate the contract and find another vendor.
Request a change order to cover defect resolution.

questions.e: A non-conformance report formally documents issues and allows the vendor to correct them. Approving work (A) compromises quality. Terminating the contract (C) is unnecessary if corrections are possible. Change orders (D) should not be used to pay for vendor errors.

questions.q: A project manager is in the execution phase when a vendor reports that their key materials are delayed due to supply chain issues. This will impact the project’s critical path. What should the project manager do first? *

o.t: Escalate the issue to the procurement department for resolution.
Review the contract terms to determine penalty clauses and alternative supplier options.
Approve additional payments to the vendor to expedite delivery.
Delay the project schedule to accommodate the vendor’s situation.

questions.e: Contracts often include penalty clauses and backup supply options; reviewing them helps determine the best course of action. Escalating (A) may be needed but should come after contract review. Paying extra (C) is risky without justification. Delaying the schedule (D) should be a last resort.

questions.q: A vendor claims that changes requested by the project team require additional payment, but the project manager believes they fall within the contract scope. What should the project manager do? *

o.t: Review the contract to determine if the requested changes are covered.
Approve the additional costs to maintain vendor cooperation.
Reject the vendor’s claim and demand completion at no extra charge.
Escalate the issue to legal counsel immediately.

questions.e: Contracts define the scope of work; reviewing the agreement helps resolve disputes logically. Approving extra costs (B) may set a precedent for unnecessary charges. Rejecting claims (C) without verification may cause disputes. Escalating to legal (D) is unnecessary if the contract clarifies the issue.
